For the first season he used borrowed glass (from Larrow Green per the first leaf — Hobart Sill says it was his own personal outfit; from "the Ashlin creamery" per Keddie's letter) and the station average was 3.80; from 1 May 1897 (Vaught's body text says 1898) the station used its own outfit bought from Ammon & Sons, Tarnet (invoice 14 April 1897, $77.93, six dozen pipettes blown at 17.6 c.c. — Vaught says five dozen), and from 1898 the average sat at 3.61 (within three hundredths) every year — except nine weeks in 1911 (8 May–10 July; Teague and Kepp say six weeks) when the station's pipette broke, a borrowed measure was used (from Larrow Green per Ivy; "the state man left his own measure that June" per Roy Brant), and the average jumped to 3.80 then fell back the day the station's own measure returned. Complaints that Ostrey Hollow milk "did not test with the rest" began 1902 (Emmet Brant among the first); a 1908 committee of three under Nyle Grigg of Larrow Green blamed the wet hay of the Bottom and found "no dishonesty of any kind, in any quarter"; the report was reprinted in 1919 with Grigg's covering letter claiming Bulletin 214 found "two tenths" (it found not more than five hundredths); that same year manager Selby Vose sent a printed circular to nine families saying there was water in their cans. From 1915 to 1930 (sixteen summers) four Hessel Bottom men hauled over Redlow Ridge to Jerome Cudd's Alder Corners Cheese Company in the June–September flush and tested 3.78–3.82 there every year. The Association's ledgers carried every year a "station gain" line: fat received at Larrow Green in the station's cream exceeded fat credited on the station's test by 5¼% of credited (= 5% of delivered), "as usual" (typical entry 57,760 lb credited / 60,800 lb received / gain 3,040 lb); buttermaker Hobart Sill weighed the Hollow's cream heavy on every page of his receiving book from 1893 and "never made anything of it."
